position: both — the 'successful' sense mostly before a noun

senses.gloss: Shining with many small flashes of light.
examples: She wore a *glittering* diamond necklace.
From the plane we could see the *glittering* lights of Las Vegas.

senses.gloss: Very successful, rich or impressive.
examples: He left a *glittering* career on Wall Street to teach high school.
It was one of the most *glittering* parties of the year.

senses.gloss: Covered with glitter or shining like it.
examples: My daughter wanted *glittery* shoes for her birthday.
The card was so *glittery* that it left sparkles all over the table.
She picked the most *glittery* dress in the store.

contrast: A false friend: Russian *глобальный* often just means 'huge' or 'large-scale' (*глобальная проблема*). English *global* means 'affecting the whole world' or 'overall' — for 'huge', say *major*, *massive* or *large-scale*.

senses.gloss: Affecting or including the whole world.
examples: *Global* warming is changing weather patterns everywhere.
The company has a *global* network of suppliers.
The pandemic was truly *global*.

senses.gloss: Covering all parts of something; overall.
examples: We need a *global* view of the budget before we cut anything.
Change the setting once and it becomes the *global* default.

senses.gloss: Dark and gray, without much light.
examples: It was a cold, *gloomy* afternoon in November.
The basement was even *gloomier* than I remembered.

senses.gloss: Sad and without hope.
examples: Why are you looking so *gloomy*?
Economists are *gloomy* about next year.
That was the *gloomiest* speech I've ever heard.

contrast: A trap for Russian speakers: *a glorified babysitter* is not *прославленная няня* — it means the job is really just babysitting, with a grander name. The meaning is always disapproving.

senses.gloss: Made to seem more important or better than it really is.
senses.ru: так называемый, всего лишь (под громким названием)
examples: My title is 'manager,' but I'm really a *glorified* secretary.
The 'resort' was a *glorified* motel with a pool.
That new phone is just a *glorified* camera.

senses.gloss: Deserving great honor and admiration.
examples: The team's *glorious* history includes six championships.
It was a *glorious* victory for the small town.

senses.gloss: Very beautiful or enjoyable.
examples: We had *glorious* weather all week.
The view from the top was *glorious*.
It was the most *glorious* sunset I've ever seen.

senses.gloss: Smooth and shiny.
examples: The horse had a *glossy* black coat.
Do you want the prints *glossy* or matte?
Her hair looked *glossier* after the treatment.

senses.gloss: Of magazines and ads: printed on shiny paper and made to look attractive and expensive.
examples: The campaign sent out a *glossy* brochure.
She works for a *glossy* fashion magazine in New York.

position: both — the 'praise' sense mostly before a noun

senses.gloss: Giving off a steady light or heat without flames.
examples: We sat around the *glowing* coals of the campfire.
The clock's hands are *glowing* in the dark.

senses.gloss: Full of praise.
examples: The restaurant got a *glowing* review in the Times.
Her boss wrote her a *glowing* recommendation.
I've never read a more *glowing* report card.

senses.gloss: Looking healthy, happy or excited.
examples: She came back from vacation tan and *glowing*.
His face was *glowing* with pride.

ru: прилипший, прикованный (к экрану и т. п.)
contrast: *The pieces were glued together* is the passive of the verb *glue*. The adjective is the informal 'can't look away' use: *glued to the TV*.

senses.gloss: Watching or paying attention to something so closely that you cannot stop.
examples: The kids were *glued* to the TV all morning.
She's been *glued* to her phone since dinner.
Everyone stayed *glued* to their seats until the last minute.

senses.gloss: Sad and quiet, often because things have gone wrong.
examples: The players looked *glum* after the loss.
Why the *glum* face?
He got *glummer* as the evening went on.

senses.gloss: Eating, or wanting, far too much.
examples: After a *gluttonous* Thanksgiving dinner, we all fell asleep on the couch.
I felt a little *gluttonous* ordering a second dessert.
The company's *gluttonous* appetite for data worries privacy groups.

form: -ed from *gnarl*, a hard knot in wood

senses.gloss: Twisted, rough and full of knots, usually because of age.
examples: A *gnarled* old oak stood in the middle of the field.
My grandfather's hands were *gnarled* from years of farm work.
The olive trees get more *gnarled* every year.

form: -y from *gnarl*, a hard knot in wood
contrast: In American slang *gnarly* started with surfers and can mean 'dangerous,' 'gross' or even 'awesome' — the tone tells you which.

senses.gloss: Twisted and full of knots.
examples: He carved a walking stick from a *gnarly* branch.
The *gnarly* roots had pushed up the sidewalk.

senses.gloss: Slang: difficult, dangerous or disgusting.
examples: That was a *gnarly* wave — I almost went under.
He has a *gnarly* scar on his knee from the crash.
The trail got *gnarlier* after the rain.

comparison: not gradable — an extreme word, like *terrible*
contrast: Informal, and some religious people find it offensive. Also written *godawful*.

senses.gloss: Very bad or unpleasant.
examples: What's that *god-awful* smell?
We had to get up at some *god-awful* hour to catch the flight.
The coffee at that place is *god-awful*.

senses.gloss: Religious and trying to live a good, moral life.
examples: They were hardworking, *god-fearing* people.
She raised her children in a *god-fearing* home.
My grandparents were more *god-fearing* than my parents.

contrast: Rude, and offensive to many religious people. Also spelled *goddam* and *goddamned*. Before another adjective it is an adverb: *It's goddamn cold*.

senses.gloss: Used to show anger or annoyance, or just to add force.
examples: Turn off that *goddamn* alarm!
I can't find my *goddamn* keys.
It's a *goddamn* shame what happened to them.

senses.gloss: Far from everything, empty and unpleasant.
examples: Why would anyone build a house in this *godforsaken* desert?
The bus left us in some *godforsaken* town at two in the morning.
It was the most *godforsaken* place I've ever worked.

senses.gloss: Not believing in God, or not following religious rules — usually said disapprovingly.
examples: The preacher warned against a *godless* society.
Some of his neighbors thought the family was *godless*.
Critics called the new movie *godless* and violent.

senses.gloss: Like a god in power, beauty or skill.
examples: Fans treated the quarterback as a *godlike* figure.
In the old myths, the heroes had almost *godlike* strength.
To a five-year-old, a teenager can seem *godlike*.

contrast: An *-ly* adjective, not an adverb: *a godly man*, never *He lived godly*. *Ungodly* is common in *at an ungodly hour* ('very early').

senses.gloss: Religious and living a moral life.
examples: She was a kind and *godly* woman.
The pastor urged us to lead *godly* lives.
He thought he was *godlier* than everyone else in town.

position: attributive only — but after a noun it means 'available': *the best deal going*

senses.gloss: Usual or current at the moment — used in *the going rate* and *the going price*.
examples: What's the *going* rate for a babysitter these days?
He paid well below the *going* price for the car.

senses.gloss: Of a business: working and making money — in *a going concern*.
examples: They sold the bakery as a *going* concern.
Within two years the startup was a *going* concern.

senses.gloss: Informal, after a noun: available or existing.
examples: This is the best pizza *going* in Chicago.
Are there any jobs *going* at your company?

contrast: *A gold ring* is made of gold — that is the noun used before another noun. As an adjective *gold* names the color; *golden* is the more literary word for it (*golden hair*).

senses.gloss: Having the deep yellow color of gold.
examples: The trees turn red and *gold* in October.
The walls of the lobby were painted *gold*.
The logo is *gold* on a black background.

contrast: Hyphenated before a noun (*a golden-brown crust*), but usually two words after a verb: *Bake until golden brown*.

senses.gloss: Of a warm brown color with yellow in it, especially food that is well cooked.
examples: The pie had a *golden-brown* crust.
Fry the onions until they are *golden brown*.
She had long *golden-brown* hair.

contrast: *She is gone* describes a state — she is not here now. *She has gone to work* is the present perfect of the verb *go*.

senses.gloss: No longer here; having left.
examples: By the time I got to the station, the train was *gone*.
How long will you be *gone*?

senses.gloss: Used up, or no longer existing.
examples: The cookies are all *gone*.
The old diner on Main Street is *gone* now.

senses.gloss: Dead — a gentle way to say it.
examples: Their father has been *gone* five years now.
It's hard to believe she's really *gone*.

contrast: Also a noun: *He's a good-for-nothing*.

senses.gloss: Lazy and useless.
examples: Her *good-for-nothing* brother never paid her back.
Get off the couch, you *good-for-nothing* bum!
The landlord called his tenants *good-for-nothing* freeloaders.

senses.gloss: Kind and wanting to help other people.
examples: He's a *good-hearted* guy who would do anything for you.
The neighbors were poor but *good-hearted*.
She's the most *good-hearted* person I know.

contrast: American spelling *humored*; British *good-humoured*.

senses.gloss: Friendly and cheerful, and not easily annoyed.
examples: The crowd was noisy but *good-humored*.
He took all the teasing in a *good-humored* way.
She was more *good-humored* about the delay than I was.

senses.gloss: Kind, friendly and patient; not meant to hurt.
examples: Our dog is big but very *good-natured*.
It was just some *good-natured* joking between friends.
He's the most *good-natured* kid in the class.

contrast: Disapproving, and more often a noun: *Don't be such a goody-goody*.

senses.gloss: Too eager to follow the rules and please people in charge.
examples: I was the *goody-goody* kid who always did her homework.
His *goody-goody* act fooled the teachers but not us.
She's a lot less *goody-goody* than she seems.

senses.gloss: Soft and sticky.
examples: The brownies are still *gooey* in the middle.
The kids' hands were covered in *gooey* marshmallow.
These are the *gooiest* cinnamon rolls in town.

senses.gloss: Silly in a funny, harmless way.
examples: He has a *goofy* smile that makes everyone laugh.
Stop being *goofy* and eat your dinner.
That was the *goofiest* costume at the party.

contrast: *the gory details* is also used as a joke about any private story: *Tell me all the gory details of your date*.

senses.gloss: Full of blood and violence.
examples: The movie was too *gory* for the kids.
He described the accident in *gory* detail.
This is the *goriest* horror film I've ever seen.

senses.gloss: Liking to talk about other people's private lives, or full of that kind of talk.
examples: Our *gossipy* neighbor knows everything about everyone.
The book is a *gossipy* account of old Hollywood.
The office got more *gossipy* after the layoffs.

senses.gloss: Having the power to control or run an organization or country.
examples: The NCAA is the *governing* body for college sports.
The *governing* party lost its majority in the election.
Safety is the *governing* principle behind every decision we make.

senses.gloss: Relating to a government.
examples: The report was written by a *governmental* agency.
They get no *governmental* funding at all.
The project needs approval at several *governmental* levels.

contrast: Russian *грациозный* is *graceful*, not *gracious*. *Gracious* is about kind, polite behavior.

senses.gloss: Moving in a smooth, attractive way, or having a pleasing shape.
examples: The dancers were incredibly *graceful*.
The bridge has long, *graceful* curves.
Cats are more *graceful* than dogs.

senses.gloss: Polite and calm in a hard situation.
examples: The senator gave a *graceful* speech after losing the race.
She found a *graceful* way to say no.

contrast: A false friend: *gracious* is not *грациозный* — that is *graceful*. *Gracious* describes kind, polite behavior. *Good gracious!* is an old-fashioned exclamation.

senses.gloss: Kind, polite and generous, especially to guests or to people with less power.
examples: Thank you for being such a *gracious* host.
She was *gracious* in defeat and congratulated the winner.
He was more *gracious* than I expected.

senses.gloss: Comfortable and elegant, as enjoyed by rich people.
examples: The hotel is famous for its *gracious* Southern style.
They live in a *gracious* old house near the park.

senses.gloss: Happening slowly, a little at a time.
examples: There has been a *gradual* improvement in her health.
The change was so *gradual* that nobody noticed it.
Doctors recommend a more *gradual* return to exercise.

senses.gloss: Of a slope: not steep.
examples: The trail has a *gradual* climb for the first mile.
The ramp is *gradual* enough for wheelchairs.

contrast: In the US *graduate school* is study after a bachelor's degree — магистратура or аспирантура, not school for graduates of high school. The adjective is pronounced GRAJ-oo-uht; the verb *graduate* is GRAJ-oo-ayt. Don't confuse it with *graduated*, which describes something marked in steps (*a graduated scale*).

senses.gloss: Relating to university study done after a first (bachelor's) degree.
examples: She's a *graduate* student in chemistry at Berkeley.
He applied to three *graduate* programs.
The university offers *graduate* courses at night.

senses.gloss: Of a photo or video: not clear, with many small spots.
examples: The only evidence is a *grainy* security video.
The photos got *grainier* as it got dark.

senses.gloss: Having a rough texture with small hard pieces.
examples: The sauce turned *grainy* when I heated it too fast.
This bread has a nice *grainy* texture.

position: both — sense 1 only before a noun

senses.gloss: Relating to grammar.
examples: The essay had a few *grammatical* errors.
We studied the *grammatical* structure of the sentence.

senses.gloss: Following the rules of grammar.
examples: Is this sentence *grammatical*?
It's *grammatical*, but no native speaker would say it.

position: both — sense 3 only before a noun
contrast: *Grand* is also informal for a thousand dollars — that's a noun: *It cost five grand*.

senses.gloss: Large, beautiful and impressive.
examples: The hotel has a *grand* staircase in the lobby.
Their new house is even *grander* than the old one.
It was the *grandest* wedding the town had ever seen.

senses.gloss: Very ambitious; planned on a large scale.
examples: He had *grand* plans to travel the world.
The city is thinking about growth on a *grand* scale.

senses.gloss: Total or most important — in fixed phrases like *grand total* and *grand prize*.
examples: That comes to a *grand* total of $312.
She won the *grand* prize in the state science fair.

contrast: A false friend: Russian *грандиозный* is usually praise (*grand*, *magnificent*, *huge*). English *grandiose* is disapproving — too big, too showy, or too ambitious to be realistic.

senses.gloss: Too big, showy or ambitious, often in a way that seems silly or unrealistic.
examples: The mayor announced another *grandiose* plan that nobody could pay for.
His ideas about himself are a little *grandiose*.
Each building was more *grandiose* than the last.

senses.gloss: Made of small grains or pieces.
examples: Spread the *granular* fertilizer evenly over the lawn.
The soil here is dry and *granular*.

senses.gloss: Very detailed; broken into small parts.
examples: We need more *granular* data to see what's going on.
The app gives you *granular* control over your privacy settings.

senses.gloss: In the form of small grains — especially ordinary white sugar.
examples: Add one cup of *granulated* sugar and stir.
You can use *granulated* garlic instead of fresh.
Make sure the coffee is finely *granulated* before brewing.

position: both — sense 2 only before a noun
contrast: *Graphic* about violence or sex means shockingly detailed. *Graphical* is only about charts and computer displays (*a graphical user interface*).

senses.gloss: Showing or describing something, especially violence or sex, in very clear and shocking detail.
examples: The show contains *graphic* violence.
She gave a *graphic* description of the attack.
The book is even more *graphic* than the movie.

senses.gloss: Relating to drawing, design or pictures.
examples: He works as a *graphic* designer.
The museum has a large collection of *graphic* art.

senses.gloss: Using or relating to pictures, charts or images, especially on a computer screen.
examples: Windows uses a *graphical* user interface.
The results are shown in *graphical* form.
The software turns raw numbers into a *graphical* report.

senses.gloss: Always trying to get more money or power for yourself.
examples: His *grasping* relatives showed up as soon as he won the lottery.
The landlord was cold and *grasping*.
She was the most *grasping* politician in the state.

contrast: The noun is usually two words: *support from the grass roots*.

senses.gloss: Started or run by ordinary people rather than by leaders or big organizations.
examples: The park was saved by a *grassroots* campaign.
She began her career as a *grassroots* organizer in Detroit.
Their fundraising is mostly *grassroots*.

senses.gloss: Covered with grass.
examples: We had a picnic on a *grassy* hill.
The backyard is *grassy* and flat.
Park on the *grassiest* part of the lot.

contrast: *gratified* is the person who is pleased; *gratifying* is what pleases: *I was gratified by the results* — *The results were gratifying*.

senses.gloss: Pleased and satisfied, especially because of something you did.
examples: We were *gratified* by the response from the community.
She was *gratified* to see her students succeed.
I was *gratified* that so many people came.

contrast: *gratifying* is what pleases you; *gratified* is how you feel: *The work is gratifying* — *I feel gratified*.

senses.gloss: Giving a feeling of satisfaction and pleasure.
examples: Teaching is hard but very *gratifying* work.
It's *gratifying* to see the garden finally bloom.
Winning this award is the most *gratifying* moment of my career.

form: -ing from *grate* ('to rub with a harsh noise')
contrast: Also a noun: *a grating* is a metal frame of bars over a hole or window.

senses.gloss: Of a sound: harsh and unpleasant.
examples: The door made a *grating* noise every time it opened.
Her laugh is loud and a little *grating*.

senses.gloss: Annoying, especially after a while.
examples: His constant bragging gets *grating* after an hour.
The most *grating* thing about the ad is that song.

contrast: Also an adverb after a verb: *They did the work gratis*. Formal or humorous; in everyday speech Americans say *free*.

senses.gloss: Given or done without charge.
examples: Drinks for the band are *gratis*.
The first consultation is *gratis*.
Parking was *gratis* for anyone with a ticket.

contrast: Not 'grateful' and, in everyday use, not 'free': *gratuitous* means done for no good reason. It is related to *gratuity* ('a tip'), but the meanings have split.

senses.gloss: Not necessary and without a good reason, often in a way that offends people.
examples: Critics complained about the *gratuitous* violence in the film.
That insult was completely *gratuitous*.
Each sequel was more *gratuitous* than the last.

contrast: Also a noun: *a grave* — могила.

senses.gloss: Very serious and worrying.
examples: The patient is in *grave* danger.
Leaving the door unlocked was a *grave* mistake.
Climate change is one of the *gravest* threats we face.

senses.gloss: Looking or sounding serious and worried.
examples: The doctor came in with a *grave* expression.
His voice was *grave* when he called.

contrast: An *-ly* adjective, not an adverb, and spelled with *ll*: *gravel* + *-ly*.

senses.gloss: Of a voice: low and rough.
examples: He had a deep, *gravelly* voice from years of smoking.
Her voice gets more *gravelly* when she's tired.

senses.gloss: Covered with or full of small stones.
examples: We drove slowly down the *gravelly* road.
The riverbank is *gravelly* and hard to walk on.

senses.gloss: Relating to gravity.
examples: The moon's *gravitational* pull causes the tides.
Scientists detected *gravitational* waves for the first time in 2015.
Jupiter's *gravitational* field is much stronger than Earth's.

contrast: American spelling *gray*; British *grey-haired*.

senses.gloss: Having gray or white hair.
examples: A *gray-haired* woman opened the door.
My dad was completely *gray-haired* by forty.
The audience was mostly *gray-haired* retirees.

contrast: American spelling *grayish*; British *greyish*.

senses.gloss: Slightly gray.
examples: The sky was a *grayish* blue.
His skin looked *grayish* and he said he felt sick.
The water turned *grayish* after the storm.

contrast: *like greased lightning* is an idiom for 'extremely fast'.

senses.gloss: Covered with a thin layer of oil, fat or grease.
examples: Pour the batter into a *greased* pan.
Make sure the baking sheet is well *greased*.
He took off down the street like *greased* lightning.

senses.gloss: Covered with oil or grease, or producing too much natural oil.
examples: Wash your *greasy* hands before you touch anything.
My hair gets *greasy* if I don't wash it every day.
His overalls were even *greasier* than his hands.

senses.gloss: Of food: cooked with too much oil or fat.
examples: We stopped at a *greasy* diner off the highway.
Those were the *greasiest* fries I've ever eaten.

takes: *at* + noun or *-ing* (sense 4); *with* + people or things (sense 4); *for* + who or what it helps
contrast: In everyday speech *a great house* is a wonderful house, not a big one — use *big* or *large* for size. *Great* for size is mostly formal or fixed (*the Great Lakes*, *a great number*). Russian *великий* matches only sense 3.

senses.gloss: Very good; excellent.
examples: We had a *great* time at the beach.
You look *great* in that jacket!
This is the *greatest* pizza in the city.

senses.gloss: Large in amount, degree or size.
examples: She spoke with *great* care.
A *great* number of people lost their homes.
The risk is *greater* than we thought.

senses.gloss: Important, famous and admired.
examples: Lincoln was one of the *great* presidents.
Many people call him the *greatest* boxer of all time.

senses.gloss: Very skilled at something, or very good for someone.
examples: She's *great* at math.
He's *great* with kids.
This park is *great* for families.

contrast: American spelling *Greco-*; British often *Graeco-*.

senses.gloss: Relating to both ancient Greece and ancient Rome, or to a style of wrestling that allows no holds below the waist.
examples: The museum has a room of *Greco-Roman* sculpture.
He won a bronze medal in *Greco-Roman* wrestling.
The courthouse was built in a *Greco-Roman* style.

senses.gloss: Wanting more money, food or power than you need.
examples: The *greedy* developers tore down the old theater.
Don't be *greedy* — leave some cake for everyone else.
The more he earned, the *greedier* he got.

contrast: Russian *православный* is *Orthodox* or *Eastern Orthodox* in general; *Russian Orthodox* is the Russian church. Always capital O.

senses.gloss: Belonging to the Orthodox church of Greece or to churches that follow it.
examples: They got married in a *Greek Orthodox* church in Astoria.
Her family is *Greek Orthodox*.
The *Greek Orthodox* Easter often falls on a different Sunday.

contrast: *the green-eyed monster* is an idiom for jealousy.

senses.gloss: Having green eyes.
examples: A *green-eyed* cat sat on the windowsill.
Both of their kids are *green-eyed*.
She married a tall, *green-eyed* musician.

senses.gloss: Slightly green.
examples: The pool water looked *greenish*.
Throw out any potatoes with *greenish* skin.
After the boat ride, he looked a little *greenish*.

senses.gloss: Liking to be with other people; sociable.
examples: He's a *gregarious* guy who talks to everyone at parties.
She's much more *gregarious* than her sister.

senses.gloss: Of animals: living in groups.
examples: Sheep are *gregarious* animals.
Most parrots are highly *gregarious*.

senses.gloss: Named after one of the popes called Gregory — used in *Gregorian calendar* and *Gregorian chant*.
examples: Russia switched to the *Gregorian* calendar in 1918.
The monks still sing *Gregorian* chant every morning.
The date is given in both the Jewish and the *Gregorian* calendar.

senses.gloss: Extremely sad because someone has died or something terrible has happened.
examples: The *grief-stricken* parents spoke to reporters.
The whole town was *grief-stricken* after the fire.
He was too *grief-stricken* to speak at the funeral.

senses.gloss: Feeling deep sadness because someone has died.
examples: Neighbors brought food to the *grieving* family.
The *grieving* widow thanked everyone for coming.
She's still *grieving*, so give her some time.

contrast: Two syllables, GREE-vuhs, and spelled *-vous*. *Grievious* (GREE-vee-uhs) is a common mistake.

senses.gloss: Very serious and causing great harm or pain.
examples: Firing her without warning was a *grievous* error.
The soldier suffered *grievous* wounds in the attack.
Of all his mistakes, this was the most *grievous*.

contrast: In American English *grilled* food is cooked over flames or hot bars, usually outdoors. British *grilled* can mean cooked under the heat at the top of an oven — Americans call that *broiled*. A *grilled cheese* is a toasted cheese sandwich made in a pan.

senses.gloss: Cooked on a grill over direct heat.
examples: I'll have the *grilled* chicken salad.
The corn tastes best *grilled*.
We had *grilled* cheese sandwiches and tomato soup.

senses.gloss: Covered with a layer of dirt.
examples: The windows of the old factory were *grimy*.
He wiped his *grimy* hands on a rag.
It was the *grimiest* bus station I've ever been in.

senses.gloss: So exciting or interesting that you cannot stop watching or reading.
examples: It's a *gripping* thriller from start to finish.
The last episode was absolutely *gripping*.
Her second novel is even more *gripping* than the first.

contrast: Sounds exactly like *grizzly*, as in *a grizzly bear* — different word, different spelling.

senses.gloss: Horrible and shocking, usually because it involves death or violence.
examples: Police made a *grisly* discovery in the basement.
The details of the murder were too *grisly* to print.
It was the *grisliest* crime scene the detective had seen.

senses.gloss: Containing or covered with very small pieces of sand or stone.
senses.ru: песчаный, с песком, скрипящий на зубах
examples: The spinach was *gritty* because nobody washed it.
The floor felt *gritty* under my bare feet.

senses.gloss: Showing hard, unpleasant parts of life in a realistic way.
examples: The show is a *gritty* drama about police in Baltimore.
The new version of the movie is *grittier* and darker.

senses.gloss: Brave and determined.
examples: The team put in a *gritty* performance in the second half.
She's a *gritty* competitor who never gives up.

senses.gloss: Having gray or partly gray hair, and often looking tough and experienced.
examples: A *grizzled* old fisherman sat on the dock.
His beard was *grizzled* and untrimmed.
The team hired a *grizzled* veteran coach.

senses.gloss: Weak and unable to think clearly, because you are tired, ill or just woke up.
examples: I always feel *groggy* in the morning.
He was still *groggy* from the anesthesia.
I felt even *groggier* after the nap.

comparison: more/most — usually graded with *well*: *well groomed*, *better groomed*
contrast: *He is being groomed for the job* is the verb *groom* ('prepare someone'), not the adjective. As an adjective it usually comes with an adverb: *well groomed*, *neatly groomed*.

senses.gloss: Neat and clean in appearance, with hair and clothes cared for.
examples: The receptionist was always perfectly *groomed*.
Their poodle is *groomed* every two weeks.
He was a well-*groomed* man in a gray suit.

contrast: 1960s–70s slang; today it sounds old-fashioned or jokey.

senses.gloss: Informal and dated: fashionable, exciting and fun.
examples: My parents met at a *groovy* little club in San Francisco.
That's a *groovy* shirt, man.
It was the *grooviest* party of the summer of '69.

position: both — senses 2 and 3 mostly before a noun
contrast: *Gross* 'disgusting' is very common informal American English. *Gross* income is before taxes and costs are taken out; *net* is after.

senses.gloss: Informal: very unpleasant; disgusting.
examples: Ew, that's so *gross*!
There was a *gross* smell coming from the fridge.
That's the *grossest* thing I've ever seen.

senses.gloss: Total, before taxes or costs are taken away.
examples: Our *gross* income last year was about $80,000.
The movie's *gross* earnings passed $1 billion.

senses.gloss: Very serious and clearly wrong.
examples: The hospital was sued for *gross* negligence.
That's a *gross* exaggeration.

senses.gloss: Strange and ugly in a way that is frightening or funny.
examples: The church roof is decorated with *grotesque* stone faces.
The masks were even more *grotesque* up close.

senses.gloss: Shocking and offensive because it is so unfair or extreme.
examples: The CEO's pay is *grotesque* compared to what the workers earn.
It was a *grotesque* abuse of power.

senses.gloss: In a bad mood and complaining a lot.
examples: Don't talk to Dad before his coffee — he's *grouchy*.
Our *grouchy* old neighbor yells at kids on his lawn.
She gets *grouchier* when she's hungry.

senses.gloss: Using completely new methods or ideas, and very important.
examples: She won the prize for her *groundbreaking* research on cancer.
The show was *groundbreaking* for its time.
It may be the most *groundbreaking* album of the decade.

senses.gloss: Not based on facts or good reasons.
examples: The accusations turned out to be *groundless*.
Your fears are completely *groundless*.
He filed a *groundless* lawsuit against his neighbor.

contrast: American spelling with one *l*; British *grovelling*.

senses.gloss: Trying too hard to please someone or to say sorry, in a way that lacks self-respect.
examples: He sent her a *groveling* apology the next morning.
I can't stand his *groveling* attitude toward the boss.
Each letter was more *groveling* than the last.

senses.gloss: Increasing in size, amount or strength.
examples: A *growing* number of people work from home.
There is *growing* concern about the cost of housing.
He's a *growing* boy, so he eats a lot.

contrast: *a grown man* stresses that someone is an adult, often in criticism: *a grown man crying over a video game*. Before a noun it is close to *grownup*, but *grown* after a verb usually needs *fully*: *The puppies are fully grown*.

senses.gloss: Fully developed; adult.
examples: They have three *grown* children.
He's a *grown* man — he can make his own decisions.
The trees will be fully *grown* in ten years.

contrast: Also spelled *grown-up*. The noun is the same word: *Ask a grownup*.

senses.gloss: Adult, or behaving in a mature way.
examples: They have two *grownup* daughters.
You're acting very *grownup* today.
She seemed more *grownup* than the other girls in her class.

senses.gloss: Dirty.
examples: Keep your *grubby* hands off my laptop!
The kids came in from the yard *grubby* and happy.
He wore the *grubbiest* sneakers I've ever seen.

senses.gloss: Morally unpleasant or dishonest.
examples: She wanted nothing to do with the *grubby* world of politics.
It was a *grubby* little scheme to make money.

senses.gloss: Given or felt unwillingly.
examples: Over time he earned the *grudging* respect of his rivals.
Her praise was *grudging* at best.
The union gave its *grudging* approval to the deal.

contrast: American spelling with one *l*; British *gruelling*.

senses.gloss: Very hard and tiring over a long time.
examples: After a *grueling* twelve-hour shift, she fell asleep in the car.
The last mile of the race was *grueling*.
Law school was the most *grueling* three years of my life.

senses.gloss: Very unpleasant and shocking, usually because it involves death or injury.
examples: The crash left a *gruesome* scene on the highway.
Some of the photos were too *gruesome* to show.
It was one of the most *gruesome* murders in the city's history.

senses.gloss: Of a voice: low and rough.
examples: "Who's there?" asked a *gruff* voice.
His voice got *gruffer* as he got older.

senses.gloss: Unfriendly or impatient in manner, though often not unkind underneath.
examples: The coach seems *gruff*, but the players love him.
She gave a *gruff* reply and went back to work.

senses.gloss: Easily annoyed and in a bad mood.
examples: I'm always *grumpy* when I don't get enough sleep.
A *grumpy* waiter threw the menus on our table.
He's the *grumpiest* man on the block.
